clue.text: Eye recognition of arse-lickers imbibing a port

indicators.note: imbibing is drinking something in, so one piece is swallowed inside the other

blocks.note: Private Eye awards its mock honour, the Order of the Brown Nose, to sycophants
taken as written

explanation.surface: Private Eye's honour for toadies is shown drinking a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the drink after 'imbibing', but it is a harbour town. Oban is a ferry port on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a Scottish harbour town and ferry terminal, so it is an example of a port.

clue.text: Where Napoleon croaked: "Bugger the sane left inside!"

indicators.note: to bugger something up is to wreck it, so the letters are thrown into disorder
inside places the abbreviation within the other letters before they are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: The exiled Napoleon's dying curse, raging against the sane people locked in with him.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks only dress up the surface; they carry no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon died in exile on St Helena, a remote British island in the South Atlantic, in 1821.

clue.text: Atrocity that's unconventional

blocks.note: first meaning: an act of wartime savagery
second meaning: an act that breaks the Geneva Conventions on the conduct of war

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unconventional' usually means quirky; here it means against the Conventions, the international treaties governing war.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaches of the Geneva Conventions are legally termed by this phrase, and they are atrocities committed in armed conflict.

clue.text: Sweats on a leading Tory blowing top

definitions.note: a plural standing for a singular noun: the fever is known by its bouts of sweating

indicators.note: blowing your top normally means losing your temper; here the top is lost, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: William Hague led the Conservative Party from 1997 to 2001

explanation.surface: A senior Conservative breaks into a sweat as he loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: HAGUE loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ague is a fever, typically malarial, marked by fits of shivering and sweating.

clue.text: Our Brenda lets one drop, being an Essex woman once, you might say

definitions.text: an Essex woman once, you might say

indicators.note: letting something drop means losing it, so one letter falls away from the name

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, the second monarch of that name
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: The Queen breaks wind in the manner of a brash Essex girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lets one drop' sounds like flatulence; it removes one numeral I from the monarch's title. 'Essex woman' is fair, as the Earl of Essex was her favourite, with 'you might say' owning up to the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Elizabeth was the lover, by repute, of Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, so loosely she was his woman.

clue.text: Edwina Currie: zany, exciting, moody, always tops? Actually, a superficial, most irritating thing

indicators.note: the tops of words are their first letters, so each word supplies only its opening one

blocks.clueFragment: Edwina Currie: zany, exciting, moody, always
blocks.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A gushing tribute to the former Tory minister Edwina Currie, undercut with the verdict that she is merely a shallow irritant.
explanation.walkthrough: Edwina Currie was a Conservative health minister. The joke is that the superficial irritant described is a skin complaint, not the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Eczema is an itchy inflammation of the skin's surface, so it is a superficial and very irritating complaint.

clue.text: Mo bets Dotty is getting head from Robin Hood …

indicators.note: dotty means crazy, so the letters before it are to be scrambled madly
the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be scrambled
the first letter of Robin

explanation.surface: A gambler called Mo is placing crazy bets on advice from the outlaw of Sherwood Forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robin Hood' reads as one name, but it splits: Robin supplies a letter and Hood alone is the definition. The ellipsis leads into the next clue for surface effect only.
explanation.definitionFit: Hood is slang, mostly American, for a gangster or criminal thug, short for hoodlum.

clue.text: More than half of Al-Fayed mug shot for a Mediterranean resort

indicators.note: more than half keeps the larger front part of the name and drops the rest
something shot is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: Mohamed Al-Fayed, then owner of Harrods and a frequent Private Eye target
taken as written

explanation.surface: A police mug shot of the Harrods owner, taken for a Mediterranean holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Four of the seven letters is more than half, so ALFA is kept and mixed with MUG. 'Mug shot' reads as one phrase but splits into fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Magaluf is a Majorcan beach town notorious for British package holidays, so it is a Mediterranean resort.

clue.text: Parties of Right getting round politicians

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
O is round in shape
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: Right-wing political parties gather around their elected members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parties' and 'politicians' push towards politics; 'round' looks like it encircles something but just supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Romps are boisterous bouts of fun, so a romp is a lively party or frolic.

clue.text: … Nigel's off getting gobbled by a cold Divine

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled and changed, so the name's letters are rearranged
what is gobbled ends up inside the eater, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: taken as written
the name's letters, rearranged
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Following on from the clue before, a man named Nigel has gone bad and been eaten by a divine figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like the name of the drag star, but it is the definition. A + C forms the outside, with the jumbled name inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelic and divine both describe something heavenly or saintly, so they are adjective synonyms.

clue.text: Colt possibly starts to gyrate, ejaculating a sticky mess

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their opening letters, so each of them gives just one

blocks.note: a Colt is a make of revolver; 'possibly' marks it as one example of a firearm
first letter of gyrate
first letter of ejaculating

explanation.surface: A young horse thrashes about and leaves a gooey mess, in typical Private Eye smut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colt' pushes towards a young horse; here it is the gun maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunge is British slang for any unpleasant sticky, slimy substance, so it is a synonym for a sticky mess.

clue.text: 'Ming' element of political leader not quite accepting acknowledgement of tabloid editor once

indicators.note: something not quite complete is short of its end, so the final letter goes
to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: Ming is the nickname of Sir Menzies Campbell, Liberal Democrat leader 2006-07; his first name is the part of him the nickname shortens
ack is the short form for acknowledgement, as in radio or computer signals

explanation.surface: A Lib Dem leader thanks a former red-top editor, the kind of political-media mix Private Eye loves.
explanation.walkthrough: Menzies is pronounced 'Mingis', hence the nickname. 'Element' looks chemical but just means part of the leader's name. Kelvin MacKenzie edited The Sun from 1981 to 1994.
explanation.definitionFit: Kelvin MacKenzie was the notorious former editor of The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper.

clue.text: (& 28ac.) Control on competition didn't happen, to Brown's relief

definitions.note: not a synonym but a description: in 2007 Gordon Brown became Labour leader unopposed, so this event never took place

blocks.note: leadership is being in control or command
a contest is a competition

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown was relieved that no challenge to his control was ever mounted.
explanation.walkthrough: '(& 28ac.)' says the answer runs on into 28 across. The second part of the clue is an extended description of the answer: when Blair stood down in 2007, no one stood against Brown.
explanation.definitionFit: A leadership contest is the internal election a party holds to choose its leader, which Brown avoided by being the only candidate.

clue.text: Tina sadly coming to see what Labour's Millennium celebrations turned out be

definitions.text: what Labour's Millennium celebrations turned out be

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the name's letters are put out of order

blocks.note: the name's letters, rearranged
coming in the sexual sense is reaching a climax

explanation.surface: A woman named Tina comes to view the Millennium Dome and finds it as disappointing as everyone else did.
explanation.walkthrough: The Millennium Dome, Labour's flagship 2000 celebration in London, was widely judged a costly flop.
explanation.definitionFit: An anticlimax is a disappointing letdown after a build-up, which is how the Dome's opening year was seen.

clue.text: Pop group consists of a group of alcoholics restraining two bastards, euphemistically

indicators.note: restraining something means holding it in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous
a euphemistic writer prints a swear word as just its initial, b----, so two of them make two Bs

explanation.surface: A band turns out to be a recovery group keeping a couple of nasty men in check.
explanation.walkthrough: Newspapers once printed rude words as an initial and dashes; that habit gives the middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Abba was the Swedish pop group that won Eurovision in 1974 with Waterloo, so it is an example of a pop group.

clue.text: Overpaid bosses owning a corporation on show

blocks.note: corporation is old slang for a big belly, so someone who has one is plump
Cats is the long-running Lloyd Webber musical, a show that was on for years

explanation.surface: Grossly paid executives who own a company parade it for display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a business, which suits the bosses, but here it is the old joke word for a paunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Fat cats is the scornful idiom for wealthy executives paid far more than they are worth.

clue.text: Writ issued by inferior ghost writer? Name one

blocks.note: sub- means below or inferior, as in substandard
Edgar Allan Poe wrote tales of the supernatural
N is the abbreviation for name
a means one, as in a dozen

explanation.surface: A legal writ served on behalf of a second-rate ghostwriter, with a demand to name names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ghost writer' looks like someone writing books under another's name; it is an author of ghost stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A subpoena is a court writ ordering a person to appear, typically as a witness.

clue.text: It shows the error of sticking arse in between expressions of hesitation

indicators.note: sticking one thing in between others places it in the middle of them

blocks.note: the first hesitant noise, er
an arse and a rat are both insults for a contemptible person
the second hesitant noise, um

explanation.surface: A note admitting a mistake caused by someone stammering rudely between ums and ers.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'expressions' supplies two separate sounds, one on each side of the inserted word.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is a correction slip or note listing a mistake in a printed text, so it shows the error.

clue.text: Pissing broadcast "doing a Brenda"

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: it's pissing down is British slang for heavy rain

explanation.surface: A crude broadcaster describes the Queen in the middle of urinating.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so doing a Brenda is doing what a monarch does.
explanation.definitionFit: A queen's job is to reign, so doing what Brenda does is ruling as monarch.

clue.text: Suckers want sexy cop picture starring Hugh Grant?

blocks.note: a mug is a gullible person, a sucker
hot means sexy

explanation.surface: Gullible fans crave a steamy police film with Hugh Grant in the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cop picture' sounds like a police thriller; it is a police photograph. Hugh Grant was famously photographed after his 1995 arrest in Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: A mugshot is the police photograph taken on arrest, and Hugh Grant's from 1995 was published worldwide.

clue.text: Hand-picked, hard boiled member of Bush's team?

definitions.text: Hand-picked, hard boiled member of Bush's team?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a grain that is harvested by hand and cooked in boiling water
the setter's reading: a tough, personally chosen member of George W. Bush's administration

explanation.walkthrough: Condoleezza Rice was Bush's national security adviser and then Secretary of State; the cereal shares her name, so every description fits both.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is both a grain picked by hand and boiled, and the surname of a hard-nosed Bush appointee.

clue.text: Arsehole's drink taken without stirring etc.

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters of the abbreviation are reordered
without here means outside, so the drink is wrapped around the other letters

blocks.note: rum is a drink
the three letters of the abbreviation, mixed

explanation.surface: A boorish man drinks his spirit neat, without stirring in anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without stirring' reads as neat; 'without' means outside, and 'stirring' acts on the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The rectum is the final section of the large intestine ending at the anus, the anatomical sense of arsehole.

clue.text: Monica finally taking Bill's lead on what happened to her dress — that won't increase the vote

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the name before it
a lead is what goes in front, so the name's opening letter is taken

blocks.note: last letter of Monica
first letter of Bill
Monica Lewinsky's blue dress was famously marked during her affair with Bill Clinton

explanation.surface: A reprise of the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal, ending with a voter who won't add to anyone's tally.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thoughts of the impeachment vote; the definition is simply holding back from voting.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstaining means declining to cast a vote, so it adds nothing to either side's total.

clue.text: Shirty thing, Cameron's no.1, after a loony turns up

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up means reading from the bottom upwards
after sends the leader's initial to the end, behind the turned-up part
number one of a name is its first letter

blocks.note: a means one, written as the Roman numeral I
a nut is a crazy person
first letter of Cameron

explanation.surface: David Cameron's top shirt, worn after some madman shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shirty' usually means bad-tempered, which suits the loony; here it means shirt-like.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic is a loose, shirt-like garment, so it is fairly called a shirty thing.

clue.text: Tip of crabby member blue? Withdraw!

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its opening end, so its first letter is taken

blocks.note: first letter of crabby
a member is an arm or leg
feeling blue is feeling down, low in spirits

explanation.surface: A grumpy man's appendage is turning blue, and someone shouts at him to pull out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' and 'Withdraw' play on a smutty reading; member is the crossword limb.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb down is the idiom for backing off from a position or retracting a claim, so it means withdraw.

clue.text: Wow, embracing date gets you stiff!

indicators.note: embracing means holding in your arms, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: oh boy! is an exclamation of surprise, like wow
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: A smutty exclamation: cuddling your date leaves you aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' teases a rude reading; it is slang for a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff is slang for a dead person, which is a body.

clue.text: Oliver's not hard when Rex enters

definitions.note: a first name standing for a surname: Oliver North, the US marine officer of the Iran-Contra affair

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the royal letter goes into the middle of the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
R stands for rex, Latin for king, as in royal ciphers

explanation.surface: Someone called Oliver is reported as not hard, a sly dig at his performance once a king walks in.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': Oliver is NOT H with R entering. Oliver North was the Reagan aide at the centre of the Iran-Contra scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver North is the American officer famous for the Iran-Contra affair, so his first name points to his surname.

clue.text: Grass a cabinet minister on air

indicators.note: on air means spoken in a broadcast, so it is the sound that matters

blocks.note: John Reid held several Labour cabinet posts, including Home Secretary in 2006-07

explanation.surface: Snitching on a government minister during a radio or television interview.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' wants to be the verb to inform on someone; it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed is a tall waterside plant of the grass family, so it is a kind of grass.

clue.text: An opportunistic union explained in terms of such discussions?

definitions.text: An opportunistic union explained in terms of such discussions?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a political alliance or trade body formed for convenience

blocks.clueFragment: explained in terms of such discussions?
blocks.note: the setter's reading: a casual sexual encounter, which Private Eye calls discussions of a particular African nationality

explanation.walkthrough: In 1973 Private Eye reported a journalist excusing a sexual tryst as discussing an East African country's affairs; ever since, the magazine has used that phrase as its euphemism for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective completes Private Eye's stock phrase for sex, so an opportunistic union is explained as one of these discussions.

clue.text: see 12ac.
